summary: Austria is part of the Schengen Area: EU and EFTA citizens enter freely, around 60 visa-exempt nationalities can stay 90 days in any 180-day period (with the ETIAS travel authorization being phased in), and everyone else needs a Schengen short-stay visa costing €90. Longer stays run through the national Visa D or a residence title such as the Red-White-Red Card.

defaultStayWindow.text: 90 days in any rolling 180-day period, counted across the whole Schengen Area rather than per country. The day you arrive counts as the first day and the day you leave counts as the last. Leaving and coming back does not reset the allowance: on any given day, days already spent anywhere in the area during the preceding 180 still count against the 90.

source.name: European Commission — Schengen short-stay calculator (DG Migration and Home Affairs)

fee.notes: Children 6–11: €45; under 6: free. Fee set EU-wide since June 11, 2024.
For stays of 91 days up to 6 months (work assignments, seasonal work, family visits, waiting for a residence title).
Approximate combined charges. Courses over 6 months need the "Student" residence permit, collected in Austria after entering on a Visa D; proof of enrollment, funds and insurance required.

Approximate total of application, issuance and personalisation charges. Points-based residence and work title for very highly qualified workers, skilled workers in shortage occupations, and other key staff; valid 2 years and tied to one employer.

passportValidity.text: Non-EU passports must be valid for at least 3 months beyond your planned departure from the Schengen Area and have been issued within the last 10 years.

travelInsurance.text: Schengen visa applicants must hold travel medical insurance covering at least €30,000, valid across the Schengen Area for the whole stay. Visa-exempt visitors are not required to show it but border officers may ask about cover.

onwardTicket.text: Border officers may ask non-EU visitors for proof of return or onward travel and accommodation details.

proofOfFunds.text: Austria publishes no fixed daily amount: border officers assess sufficient means case by case, taking into account cash, cards, prepaid accommodation and the purpose and length of the stay.

declarations.name: EES — Entry/Exit System (biometric registration)
declarations.submitWindow: At the border on first entry
declarations.text: Non-EU travelers are registered biometrically (fingerprints and photo) in the EU Entry/Exit System at Schengen external borders. Registration happens at the border. There is nothing to submit in advance, but allow extra time on your first entry.

declarations.name: ETIAS — European Travel Information and Authorization System

fee.notes: Free for under-18s and over-70s. Valid 3 years or until passport expiry.

declarations.text: Visa-exempt travelers will need an ETIAS travel authorization to enter the Schengen Area. It is being phased in. Check the official EU site for the current status and apply only there.

currencyLimits.text: Cash of €10,000 or more (or equivalent) must be declared when entering or leaving the EU.

notes: Duty-free from outside the EU: 200 cigarettes, 1 liter of spirits, goods up to €300 (€430 arriving by air/sea).
No limits on goods for personal use when arriving from another EU country.

payments.text: Cards are widely accepted in cities and chains, but Austria keeps a strong cash culture. Many small restaurants, cafés, market stalls and mountain huts are cash-only.

safety.text: Austria is a very safe destination with low crime. Watch for pickpockets in crowded Vienna sights and on public transport; in the Alps, weather and avalanche conditions are the main seasonal risks.

source.name: U.S. Department of State — Austria Travel Advisory

bestTimeToVisit.text: May–September for cities, lakes and Alpine hiking; December for Christmas markets and the start of the ski season, which runs to March or April.

roadVignette.appliesTo: Cars, camper vans and motorbikes up to 3.5 t; prices below are for cars.

penalty.notes: Substitute toll (Ersatzmaut) for a car or camper van, payable on the spot; €100 for a motorbike. Refusing it turns into an administrative fine of €300–3,000.

roadVignette.text: Austrian motorways and expressways may only be used with a valid vignette — either the digital one tied to your number plate or the traditional sticker, which ASFINAG is selling for the last time in 2026. Buy it before you join the motorway. The Alpine section tolls (A9 Gleinalm and Bosruck, A10 Tauern and Katschberg, A11 Karawanken, A13 Brenner, S16 Arlberg) are charged separately on top of the vignette.

idp.text: Austria is a party to both the 1949 Geneva and the 1968 Vienna Conventions on Road Traffic, so it recognizes an International Driving Permit issued under either.

source.instrument: Convention on Road Traffic, Geneva, 19 September 1949 (UNTS vol. 125, p. 3); Convention on Road Traffic, Vienna, 8 November 1968 (UNTS vol. 1042, p. 17)

driving.text: Austria is a party to both the 1949 Geneva and the 1968 Vienna Conventions on Road Traffic, so it recognizes an International Driving Permit issued under either. Whether a permit is required in addition to a national license, and for how long a foreign license may be used, are set by national road law and have not been checked for Austria yet.

tips.text: The 90-day limit counts across the entire Schengen Area, not just Austria — days spent in Germany or Italy count against the same allowance.
Driving on Austrian motorways requires a vignette (€12.80 for 10 days, €106.80 for a year; digital or sticker). Buy it before joining the motorway, or pay a €200 substitute toll on the spot.
Nearly all shops and supermarkets close on Sundays and public holidays — stock up on Saturday; only bakeries, station shops and restaurants stay open.
Apply for ETIAS only at the official travel-europe.europa.eu site once it becomes mandatory — unofficial sites charge inflated fees.

faq.question: Do US citizens need a visa for Austria?
faq.answer: No. US passport holders can visit Austria and the rest of the Schengen Area visa-free for up to 90 days in any 180-day period. Once ETIAS becomes mandatory, they will need to obtain this online authorization (€20) before travel.

faq.question: How much does an Austria Schengen visa cost?
faq.answer: The Schengen short-stay visa costs €90 for adults and €45 for children aged 6–11. It allows stays of up to 90 days in any 180-day period across all Schengen countries. Austria's national Visa D for stays of 91 days to 6 months costs €150.

faq.question: What is Austria's Red-White-Red Card?
faq.answer: It is Austria's points-based residence and work title for non-EU skilled workers — very highly qualified workers, skilled workers in shortage occupations and other key staff. It is issued for 2 years, tied to one employer, and total charges come to roughly €160.

faq.question: Do I need a vignette to drive in Austria?
faq.answer: Yes. All motorways and expressways require a vignette: roughly €12 for 10 days, €30 for 2 months or €104 for a year (prices adjusted annually), as a sticker or digital vignette. Driving without one brings an on-the-spot fine of about €120.

faq.question: How long can I stay in Austria without a visa?
faq.answer: Visa-exempt non-EU visitors can stay up to 90 days within any 180-day period, counted across the whole Schengen Area. EU and EFTA citizens can stay indefinitely but must register locally after 3 months.
